title: Is there a bot that trades from your own wallet, with no API keys and a permission you can revoke yourself? I came up empty.
author: rushapoil
selftext:
By "this way" I mean these four together, not one or two of them:

- it trades on-chain from the wallet you already hold, so there is no deposit and no exchange account
- no API keys anywhere in the loop
- the permission you sign is capped, and you can revoke it yourself without asking anyone
- every fill is a transaction on a public chain, so the record is not the bot's own screen

Plenty of things have one or two. "Non-custodial" gets used loosely enough that it often just means the operator does not hold your exchange password, which is not the same claim at all.

Disclosure so nobody has to dig for it: I built one that works this way, which is exactly why I want to know what else is out there. I am not linking it and this is not a pitch. I have gone through the usual lists and the recommendations in the bot subs and I have not found a second one, and "I could not find it" is a much weaker statement than it sounds.

So: does one exist? If you know it, name it.

comments.author: trunksta
comments.body: No API keys? How's it going to communicate cup and string?

replies.author: rushapoil
replies.body:
Right, that is the distinction I was reaching for. On chain there is no API key because there is no account on someone else's server to log into. The wallet owner signs one transaction granting a spending allowance to a contract, with a cap, and can revoke it later. After that an executor can call that contract to swap within the cap, and the proceeds land back on the owner's address.

So the executor is not holding the private key. What it holds is a permission, and that permission is a public object you can read and cancel from your own wallet. It is a different trust model from an API key on an exchange, where the key is the account and the venue holds the balance. Not automatically a better one, it just fails differently, and that is the part I was asking about.

comments.author: ProposalForce
comments.body: Giving a random bot access to your wallet is a quick way to get drained

replies.author: rushapoil
replies.body:
That is the right instinct and I am not going to argue you out of it. An unlimited approval handed to a contract nobody has read is one of the most common ways people get drained, and being on chain does not fix that on its own.

What decides it is what the approval actually says: a cap you choose, one contract, and a revoke you can send yourself from the wallet without asking anyone. If any of those three is missing, your objection stands as written. That is also why I put this as a question rather than a claim, because the version worth having is the one where you can inspect the permission instead of trusting the person offering it.

comments.author: RanDumb_YouSir
comments.body: lol no that’s quite literally not how this works. To access ANYTHING on your account it’s going to require api keys

comments.author: NefariousnessOpening
comments.body:
how can you trade on a blockchain without it being public?   
I have built some systems. I usually generate the wall programmatically fund it from a treasury wallet requiring my approval and then conditions for up or down or time when met send the funds from the trading wallet to different wallet b that i sig and the trading wallet is deleted

replies.author: rushapoil
replies.body:
You cannot, and I stopped trying to. Every fill is public, and that turned out to be the part I wanted: if the record is on the chain, nobody has to take my word for what the bot did, me included.

Your pattern answers a different question and it answers it well. A fresh wallet per run, funded from a treasury that needs your approval, swept out and discarded, keeps each run isolated and keeps the treasury out of the blast radius. That is a solid design when you are the one running the system and the one holding the keys.

The case I could not solve that way is the other one: someone who is not you, who does not run your infrastructure, and who has to decide what to trust before anything has proven itself to them. A generated wallet still has a key and somebody holds it. What I ended up with instead is that the user keeps their own wallet and their own key, the permission they sign is capped and they can revoke it themselves whenever they want, and every fill lands on a public chain where a block explorer settles the argument. Public is the cost, and it buys the one thing a dashboard cannot.
